rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-1: about 135,000 full-timers at firms of 50+ FTE are offered nothing and about 105,000 are offered less than K1 requires, so K1 binds for them.

No assumption row matches; probability judged from the text of the record: employers report each employee's offer status on quarterly withholding returns and the charge is assessed with them, so a bound employer either offers or pays; the handbook's A-18 (p 0.55) has only some firms misreporting, so most comply.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-3: money wages are fixed in the short run by pay scales and yearly raises in at-will employment.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-6: wages above the minimum can adjust over the medium horizon, as raises are set.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-7: at players, for the marginal pair, cover at 30% is worth less to the worker than its cost to the employer.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-23: over the medium to long run, workers' alternatives to bound employment are clearly worse than employers' alternatives.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-21: business values reflect expected earnings, and buyers expected the Act from its introduction.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-19: insurers, unions, employer associations and the large chains can organize at a cost below their stakes.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-19, which names unions among those who can organize at a cost below their stakes; the recipients are workers at bound firms, about 6% of private employees being under collective agreements.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-9: the minimum wage binds for some workers at bound firms (11% of private employees at or near $14).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-1, which rests on the survey: about 105,000 full-timers are offered a plan that falls short on benefits or on the employer's share. (A-5, p 0.7, is the narrower premise that some of those firms upgrade rather than pay; the question asks only whether such plans exist.)
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-11: between 30 and 40 hours, extra hours from existing full-timers substitute for extra full-time heads.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-24: most competitors of mid-size bound firms in local services are bound at a material per-head cost, p = 0.4 (they are mostly small exempt firms or capped chains). The answer is no, with P(yes) 0.4.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-26: Quenby's tradable producers compete with Tarnley producers, which is not bound.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-22: firms not bound (small, compliant, capped) compete with mid-size bound firms in local product markets.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-17: contracting out and franchising are open to some firms near 50 at a cost below the term or the charge (A-34, p 0.55, gives the same figure for agency labor under the cap).
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-35: some newly covered workers are near the margin between staying and moving to an unbound job.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-14: some firms near 50 FTE value staying below the line more than the extra work.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-5: some firms with plans short of K1 upgrade them rather than pay, so the standard rules out the lean designs for them.

No assumption row matches; probability judged from the text of the record: the Department of Insurance certifies plans under K2 and keeps the list, and a plan not on it does not count under K1, so insurers that sell to bound firms submit plans that meet it.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-19: insurers can organize at a cost below their stakes.

No matching assumption in WE-036; judged from the text: firms buy plans meeting K2 because K1 counts only those plans, not because they value the benefit standard over lean plans (the demand comes from K1, C-24).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-036 (illustrative figures), A-4: some bound firms choose to pay the charge for at least some full-timers (all the capped firms, many mid-size low-wage firms).
